messages.subject: WAIC's a go!
messages.body_plain:
I sat down to sketch out how to specify WAIC
for RATS and realized we already have what we need
in the "generated quantities" block.

So all we need to add is a variable declaration for
the log likelihoods of y[n,t] (weight of rat n
at time x[t]) and then assign their log probabilities:

   generated quantities {
     double ll_y[N,T];

     for (n in 1:N)
       for (t in 1:T)
         ll_y[N,T] <- normal_log(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar),
                                 sigma_y);
   }

Just needing the log likelihood is greatly simplified
over the model itself, which is mostly boilerplate priors.

All of the data, transformed data, parameters, and
derived parameters will be in scope at the point the
generated quantities block is executed.  And that's once
per iteration, not per leapfrog step (though we should
be able to improve on that, because we don't need
the generated quantities during burnin or for
thinned iterations).

The values for ll_y[n,t] will then get written out
with the parameters and transformed parameters.
I could try to get fancy and accumulate the column
sums within Stan rather than writing them.  We could even
add a new block for waic like "generated quantities" and
treat the values created there differently.

Either way, it's going to be dead easy if we can put
the burden on the user this way to duplicate the model.

I'll create a second model, rats_waic.stan in the
same directory as rats.stan.

- Bob

PS:  Now that I look at our code for RATS, I'm pretty
      sure I have the parameters/transformed parameters
      reversed.  The variances are the parameters and
      their square roots are the transformed parameters used
      in our normal(..).  One of these days, the order of
      transformation requiring Jacobians will sink in.

      Also, transformed parameters should have constraints now
      because the ranges are checked before they're written.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] WAIC's a go!
messages.body_plain:
You did say they all needed to be normalized.

It's no problem -- we have a flag in the log
density functions that determines if it's
computed up to a proportion or not, so this
already gets compiled the right way.

It's only when you write y ~ foo(theta) in
a model that we only take the log of a probability
calculated up to a proportion.

What's cool is that the additive terms for proportionality
can be computed statically (at compile time) based
on argument types. The C++ technique for this (template
meta-programming) is described on the last slide or
two of my talk.

- Bob

messages.subject: "parallel" random number generators
messages.body_plain:
Suppose we're in the MCMC case and want to generate
four parallel Markov chains.

The theoretical concern is that if you just take four
"random" seeds, the sequence of numbers they generate
might overlap.  If you're running a whole lot of parallel
MCMC chains and the period of the random number generator (the
number of random numbers before it repeats) is small, then
there's a non-negligible chance of overlap.

The "parallel" random number generators aren't parallel
in the usual sense of thread-safe, etc.  Instead, what
they do (or at least L'Ecuyer's linear congruential generator
does) is let you efficiently skip ahead any number of
elements in the random-number sequence.  This allows you to
get "independent" samples for multiple Markov chains.  With
four chains and a total chain length of M, we can use:

   chain 1:  seed N
   chain 2:  seed N, skip ahead M/4 items
   chain 3:  seed N, skip ahead 2M/4  items
   chain 4:  seed N, skip ahead 3M/4 items

Then, each chain draws from a different part of the underlying
random number sequence starting from seed N, and are
effectively "independent".

I don't think that's much of a concern for us.
And the solutions to overcome it are relatively slow
(around 8% of the speed of faster generators).  So, what
I'm proposing is:

PROPOSED DESIGN
---------------
Mersenne Twister RNG (Boost mt19937)

Specify for each chain the base seed and chain ID
and use seed base seed + ID for the chain.

The alternative is to go with:

FANCY PANTS RNG DESIGN
----------------------
L'Ecuyer RNG (Boost ecuyer1988)

Specify for each chain the base seed, the chain ID and
the total number of chains.  Asisgn seeds to chains
as above.

- Bob

messages.subject: bug in multiply_log()
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I think I've tracked down the bug that was causing adaptation to hang in rats (and dyes? and other things?). Well, almost tracked down.

The basic issue is that the value we're computing for the gradient of the multiply_double() function is off by 2. Why this is is a bit of a mystery to me. But if you replace the multiply_log(alpha+1.0, y) call in inv_gamma_log() with (alpha+1.0)*log(y), then everything works fine.

Also: what's the deal with the different versions of multiply_log() in the stan/agrad/special_functions.hpp and stan/maths/special_functions.hpp? The first one does not seem to be getting called when gradients are computed.

Finally: can I re-check in my testGradients() function in prob_grad.hpp? It's really really useful for finding bugs like this, and it's useful if you want to code your own gradients for speed.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] "parallel" random number generators
messages.body_plain:
There are a variety of configurable random number
generators with different properties.  Sort of like
MCMC algorithms.

The two we're looking at are:

Mersenne Twister:
   reasonably fast samples
   very long cycle before repeats (2**19000)
   slow skip-ahead

L'Ecuyer:
   slower samples (8% speed of Mersenne)
   shorter cycle before repeats (2**61)
   fast skip-ahead

To absolutely guarantee non-overlap of
the sequences, you need something like L'Ecuyer.

Matt, Daniel, and I discussed it today and thought
it wasn't necessary.  But then Ben and Malecki have
been urging us to use a parallel version all along,
so we thought we might still be missing something,
hence the e-mail.

It'll have the biggest impact on performance in
simple examples like RATS where the random number
generation is a bigger proportion of the compute
time.

I could also make it configurable, but that makes
the software more complicated to write, document,
and maintain.

- Bob

messages.subject: functors for finite diffs, optimization, etc.
messages.subject_clean: functors for finite diffs, optimization, etc.
messages.body_plain:
The right way to do all of these general calls seems
to be with the C++ notion of a callable object, or
functor.  This'll be true not just for the finite diffs
stuff, but also for operations like optimization.

The signature for gradient by finite diffs would be
something like:

   template <typename Scalar, typename Function>
   S
   grad_finite_diffs(const std::vector<Scalar>& x,
                     Function& f,
                     std::vector<S>& grad);

The return is the value of the function f at x.

Functor f must be callable as follows:

     Scalar f(std::vector<Scalar>& x);

This generalizes the notion of a function pointer and
is the standard lib way to write general "algorithms"
like this in C++11.  If f is a class or struct, it'll
just implement

    Scalar operator()(std::vector<Scalar>& x);

and we're good to go (but see below for complications
due to int params in log_prob_grad).

The Scalar instances x[n] must implement
difference (Scalar - Scalar) and (Scalar + double),
the two ops involved in finite diffs.

We could limit the function to be stateless by
declaring it const.

The old C-style way of doing this would've been to
use a function pointer.

Now, in order for our prob_grad objects to play nicely,
we're going to need to use some fancy binding for the
int parameters.  One way to do this would be to add
a functor factory:

   typedef double functor_t(const std::vector<double>& x);

   functor_t get_prob_functor(const std::vector<int>& params_i);

This seems a bit complex for users, so we could actually
skip the base class prob and implement prob_grad with
finite diffs based on plain old log_prob right in the base
prob_grad class.  This'd then look just like what Matt did,
only it'd actually implement the gradient function.

    double log_prob_grad_finite_diffs(
       const std::vector<int>& params_i,
       const std::vector<double>& params_r,
       std::vector<double>& gradient);

Now we could just leave this in the base class prob_grad,
or noting that this is the same signature as the
pure virtual log_prob_grad() function, we could actually
implement it with this instead.

The clunkiness there is that you need to explicitly call
the parent class's implementation to get finite diffs
from an instance of log_prob_grad_ad.

Any preferences for how this goes?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Feb 4, 2:04 pm, Bob Carpenter <c...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> The right way to do all of these general calls seems
> to be with the C++ notion of a callable object, or
> functor.  This'll be true not just for the finite diffs
> stuff, but also for operations like optimization.

For: Functors
Against: Anything resembling old C style

Also, I would definitely be for supporting Vectors in the Eigen sense
in addition to (or maybe to the exclusion of) Vectors in the std
sense.

There is a good example of using functors with Eigen in the nonlinear
optimization module of Eigen/unsupported.

Is there a purpose for finite-diff besides checking auto-dif? Either
way, I would also nominate "complex step" approximations, which are
considered better than finite-diff primarily because finite-diff is
prone to cancellation. Both involve adding a tiny h to the parameter,
but with complex step h is on the imaginary axis. The imaginary part
of the function output divided by h is a good approximation to the
partial derivative. Google [derivative "complex step"] for more info,
particularly anything written by Nick Higham in a matrix function
context. This should be really easy in Eigen with templated parameters
because Eigen already supports mixed operations between doubles and
complex doubles. Clearly, the downside is that this is limited to
functions that do sensible things with complex numbers.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I'll tentatively vote for a functor factory method in prob_grad, since it'll be useful for multiple things. That said, I still think it's valuable to have a function that just makes sure your gradients are correct. This is not just for checking auto-diff, but also for users (like me) who want to eliminate the overhead of auto-diff by writing their own gradient implementations. (Although this could also be accomplished, with higher precision, by a function that compared the auto-diff-based base implementation of grad_log_prob() with the possibly handwritten top-level implementation of grad_log_prob().)

Most of our functions don't do sensible things with complex numbers. Which I'm pretty comfortable with. It would, however, definitely be better to use the two-sided method of finite differences rather than the one-sided version I've got in there currently. (It's twice as expensive, but you don't use finite differences because it's fast.)

Matt

> in addition to (or maybe to the exclusion of) Vectors in the std
> sense.

> optimization module of Eigen/unsupported.
>
> Is there a purpose for finite-diff besides checking auto-dif? Either
> way, I would also nominate "complex step" approximations, which are
> considered better than finite-diff primarily because finite-diff is
> prone to cancellation. Both involve adding a tiny h to the parameter,
> but with complex step h is on the imaginary axis. The imaginary part
> of the function output divided by h is a good approximation to the
> partial derivative. Google [derivative "complex step"] for more info,
> particularly anything written by Nick Higham in a matrix function
> context. This should be really easy in Eigen with templated parameters
> because Eigen already supports mixed operations between doubles and
> complex doubles. Clearly, the downside is that this is limited to
> functions that do sensible things with complex numbers.
>
> Ben

Glad we can agree on functors.  We can
template out

   std vectors: std::vector<T>
   Eigen column vectors: Eigen<T,Dynamic,1>
   Eigen row vectors: Eigen<T,1,Dynamic>
   Eigen matrices: Eigen<T,Dynamic,Dynamic>

because they all support size() and unary [] (for
matrices, size is M x N and access is column-major
by default).

Matt previously suggested that we also support
plain old (T*,size_t).  We could certainly implement
the Eigen and std::vector versions on (T*,size_t)
because they have size() and T* is just the start
iterator.  Also, instead of size_t, we can also allow
the end iterator.

    fun(T* ts, size_t length)

    fun(iterator<T>* start, iterator<T>* end)

    fun(std::vector<T>& ts);

    fun(Matrix<T,M,N>& m); // templating M&N supports all versions

I'm not sure what the cleanest most idiomatic
thing is to do here.  I'd like to support more than
Eigen types here.  Eigen<T,Dynamic,Dynamic>
has a big advantage is speed and size over
std::vector<std::vector<T> >, because the former
uses one block of contiguous memory and the latter is
a bunch of std::vector<T>, each of which has its own
size.

Ben mentioned that Eigen [] checks the range, whereas
() doesn't, so we might even want to override for
more efficiency (depends on whether we want the checks
or not).

Looks like the Eigen developers are looking for
volunteers to write an optimization module:

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/index.php?title=Todo#Optimization_module

Do you know where I could find their finite
diff implementation?

I'm trying to be conservative on dependencies.
Right now, we only depend on the supported bits of
Eigen and Boost as dependencies.

I didn't bring in the unsupported modules from
Eigen or the RNG lib Ben menitoned yet, but we can
always add more dependencies.

messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the confusing terminology.  To put
it in proper C++ lingo, functors are just
objects that implement the function-call
operator() and hence can be called like functions.
C++11 lambda expressions give you a way of
creating anonymous functor-like objects that
can be called like functions.

To define a square root callable (as opposed
to function pointer), we could use an explicitly
named functor

   struct sqrt_functor
     double operator()(double x) { return sqrt(x); }
   };

   double y = sqrt_functor(2.0);

or a C++ lambda expression:

   [](double x) { return sqrt(x); }

You can really think of [] as an anonymous way or
writing the functor's operator definition -- they use
the same definition starting at the argument
declaration (double x) (the lambda's return type is
automatically computed by the type of the return expression,
so it doesn't get declared;  thankfully they've added
an "auto" super type inference type to make dealing with
this issue).

As a simple example, we could pass either the functor
or lambda expression to a function templated on
the callable F:

   template <typename F, typename X>
   double apply(F f, X x) {
       return f(x);
   }

Now the following four expressions all return
the square root of 2:

directly apply functor:

    sqrt_functor()(2.0);

directly apply lambda expression:

    ([](double x) { return sqrt(x); })(2.0);

indirectly apply functor:

     apply(sqrt_functor(),2.0);

indirectly apply lambda expression:

     apply([](double x) { return sqrt(x); }, 2.0);

Acting like a function is an instance of what
C++ calls a "concept" -- it's the set of operations
and contexts an argument needs to be usable in to
instantiate a template.

So a finite differences method could be declared
using a templated callable and scalar as:

     template <typename F, typename S>
     S finite_diffs(F f, std::vector<S> x);

Though it's now more idiomatic to not call this kind
of thing with a vector, but with an iterator, but that
seems clunky in the context of multiple-argument functions.

The nice part of lambda expressions and functors is
that they have proper modern C++ behavior in that
they have proper value semantics, so they can be used
straightforwardly (and efficiently) without a whole
lot of reference/dereference hoo-ha.  Stan's agrad::var
is another instance of something designed to have
proper value semantics.  For simple functors like sqrt_functor,
it's even better in that the struct has no data, so it
can be treated by an optimizing compiler like a type and
no data need be passed anywhere.

Boost already provides a lot of lambda-like functionality
that I'm using for the parser to support lazy evaluation
(check out Boost's Phoenix library, which generalizes
Boost Lambda, which generalizes Boost Bind, which
generalizes pre C++99's built-in bind).  Any of these
could also be used to define an appropriate callable.

Sorry -- that took a lot of explaining.

Back to our regularly scheduled programming.

- Bob

Re: [stan-dev] compiling error for vector(M) [due to "most vexing parse"]
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] compiling error for vector(M) [due to "most vexing parse"]
messages.body_plain:
Believe it or not, there's an entire Wikipedia
page devoted to this "feature" of the C++ parser
and its unexpected consequences:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Most_vexing_parse

As the Wikipedia says, Clang gives a good error
message, which is how I found the Wikipedia entry:

src/demo/jaws.cpp:183:20: warning: parentheses were disambiguated as a
function declarator
         vector_v mu(vector_v(M));

Eh?

Lucky for us, the Wikpedia describes the magic
pixie dust required to get a more reasonable
behavior out of the constructor.  A magic layer of
parens:

         vector_v mu((vector_v(M)));

I'll commit a fix to the code generator ASAP.

The web is so awesome.

- Bob

P.S.  reminds me of Boost's recommended disambiguation
of isnan as (boost::math::isnan)(x) so that "isnan"
isn't expanded as a macro.

messages.body_plain:
Variable declarations were trickier than I thought, but the bugs
in variable declaration generation that Jiqiang
found (see mail chain below) are now patched and the compiled
models are now parsing for:

   src/models/bugs_examples/vol2/jaws/jaws.stan
   src/models/bugs_examples/vol2/mvn_orange/mvn_orange.stan

----------------

The following details are probably only interesting if
you spent the last few hours with pencil and paper and
C++ compiler.

After fixing the "most vexing parse", the problem with
which is that

   var a(var());

isn't taken as an initialization of a to var(), I
introduced a simpler, but related parsing ambiguity,
which Jiqiang also found:

   var a();    // variable a of type var
               // initialized with nullary constructor var()
   var b = a;  // OK

   double a();    // a declared as nullary function returning double
   double b = a;  // DOH!

What I needed was a slightly more nuanced base case
for the recursive generation of types:

   var a(var()); // copy constructor
   var b = a; // OK

   double a(double()); // init to default 0
   double b = a; // OK

but that was too ugly to bear, so I cleaned up the
base case so the declarations are the way I'd write
them by hand (now that I understand the ambiguities
mentioned above):

   var a;  // variable a of type var init with nullary ctor var()
   var b = a;  // OK

   double a;  // declaration of variable a
   double b = a; // OK

- Bob

On Tue, Feb 7, 2012 at 2:46 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Some of the BUGS models (like epil.stan) have
> problems in that parameters are getting transformed and
> sampled without Jacobians being applied.  I almost certainly
> committed the original sin with RATS.
>
> I fixed rats.stan, but not epil.stan and haven't looked
> for other cases.
>
> Here's an instance of the right way to deal with gamma
> priors on precision (inverse gamma priors on variance)
> in Stan.
>
>  // GOOD PROGRM
>  parameters {
>    double(0,) sigma_sq;
>  }
>  transformed parameters {
>    double(0,) sigma;
>    sigma <- sqrt(sigma_sq);
>  }
>  model {
>    sigma_sq ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
>
>    for (n in 1:N)
>      y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>  }
>
> It's OK to sample a parameter
>
>   sigma_sq ~ inf_gamma(...);
>
> and then transform it for use
>
>   sigma <- sqrt(sigma_sq);
>
>   y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>
> We wind up with:
>
>   p(sigma_sq,y) prop-to
>     InvGamma(sigma_sq|0.001,0.001)
>     * PROD_n Normal(y|mu,sqrt(sigma_sq))
>
> Remember that all parameters and transformed parameters
> are output.  If you don't want to see the sigma in
> the output, but only the sigma_sq, define sigma as a local
> variable in the model rather than as a transformed parameter.
> The effect on sampling and computation is exactly the same, only
> the I/O changes.  (I'm afraid there's no way to only write
> sigma and not sigma_sq here w/o applying the Jacobian manually.)
>
> But it's NOT OK to do it the other way around:
>
>  // BAD PROGRAM
>  parameters {
>    double(0,) sigma;
>  }
>  transformed parameters {
>    double(0,) sigma_sq;
>    sigma_sq <- square(sigma_sq);
>  }
>  model {
>    sigma_sq ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
>
>    for (n in 1:N)
>      y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>  }
>
> It's legal to transform and sample the transformed
> parameter, but ONLY if you apply the appropriate
> Jacobian determinant.  The bad program leads to
>
>  p(sigma,y) NOT prop-to
>    InvGamma(square(sigma)|0.001,0.001)
>    * PROD_n Normal(y|mu,sigma)
>
> This model could be fixed by applying the Jacobian of
> the inverse of transform:
>
>   p_sigma(sigma)
>     = p_sigma_sq(square(sigma_sq)) * | d/dx square(sigma) |
>
> which translates into Stan as another statement for the
> transformed parameters block:
>
>   lp__ <- lp__ + log(2 * sigma);
>
> or more efficiently as:
>
>   lp__ <- lp__ + log2() + log(sigma);
>
> (I just added constants like log2() yesterday.)
>
> This very prevalent use case would motivate an alternative
> parameterization of inverse gamma so we could just write:
>
>   sigma ~ square_inv_gamma(0.001,0.001)
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: puzzling Wishart behavior
messages.body_plain:
Qijiang's simple test case (thanks!) just
samples a single covariance matrix from
a Wishart with fixed parameters:

   model {
     W ~ Wishart(nu,S);
   }

with

   S = diag(2,1,0.5)
   nu = 4.0

So E[W] = diag(8,4,2) according to both Wikipedia and
BDA, but not according to Stan.  With 100K samples
(50K adaptation -- runs very fast, mixes very well),
I get posterior means for diag(W) as Qijiang reported
of (4,2,1), exactly half of (8,4,2).

Now if I take other values of nu, I get:

   nu:      4            5               20
   expect:  (8, 4, 2)    (10, 5, 2.5)    (40, 20, 10)
   got:     (4, 2, 1)    ( 6, 3, 1.5)    (35, 18, 9)

This sure looks like an off-by-two error somewhere,
so that a specification of nu=4, acts like nu=2,
whereas nu=20, acts like nu=18.

This is also consistent with NUTS stalling during
adaptation unless nu >= (K + 1), whereas Wikipedia
says nu must only be greater than or equal to (K - 1).

The results also look similar to what you'd get from
the degrees of freedom being off by two if I take
a dense (4 x 4) scale matrix.  But they also look
like what you'd get if they were half of what you'd
expect.  Neither lines up perfectly.  For instance,
here's the posterior means of the diagonals:

got: "9.2744237676"  "26.774953898"  "30.26098228"   "3.39694758585"

from scale matrix with diagonals (and lots of off-diags):

   S[1,1] <- 2.9983662;
   S[2,2] <- 11.4803610;
   S[3,3] <- 11.676181;
   S[4,4] <- 1.4482736;

nu = 5, so expecting roughly (15, 136, 151, 16)

with nu = 3 would expect     ( 9,  34,  35, 4.2)

with nu=10, we expect (30,115,117,14)

[1] "22.87012728" "84.78596754" "82.43954378" "10.29494457"

This is much more in line with the (nu-2) hypothesis.

All the formulas in the actual Wishart file look OK,
and I double checked them by rederiving on paper
from scratch and comparing to the existing implementation.
There are also quite a few unit tests that I created using
the R package MCMCpack for Wisharts.

The problem is NOT with multiply_log, as we have the
same problem with the full expression (x * log(y)).  The problem's
also not with propto, as we get the same answer with
the template parameter set to true or false (I just
edited the generated code for tests).

It is also not with burnin/adaptation, as I get the same
results with 10K, 100K or 1M samples.

I am checking in a patch to some of the propto calcs which
were wrong, but none of them affected Qijiang's original
case because we were using constant scale and dof params.
But we definitely need to get unit tests in place for all these
propto calcs.

I could use some help tracking this one down.

- Bob

messages.subject: (re)moving files in stan's tree
messages.body_plain:
Can we establish a standard operating procedure for (re)moving files?

The problem is that if Alice has made changes to a file but is not
ready to push them yet, and Bob (not Carpenter specifically but the
Bob that is not Alice) decides to rename that file, move it to a
different directory, delete it, etc., then when Alice updates the
update fails or "succeeds" and the changes go poof. Subversion was not
designed to handle such things gracefully. Thus, the traditional
advice when using subversion is to "commit to the central repository
the instant you have made a change", which mitigates the potential for
this particular problem but leads to a lot of half-baked commits.

So, I think Alice needs to say on the list something like "I am going
to (re)move the following files from ... to ... in +24 hours, so
anyone should commit any uncommitted changes to those files by then or
petition for a delay."

Ben

SVN for handling the problem of person A changing

ready to merge back to the main branch.  That doesn't
solve the problem Ben outlines, though.

Joel Spolsky wrote a nice-looking tutorial on

On Feb 8, 3:20 pm, Bob Carpenter <c...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> I've only ever used CVS or SVN.  Google also

Google code doesn't support git directly, although since the last time
I complained about subversion, I started using git-svn. This basically
means I am using git locally and a bidirectional bridge between git
and svn to update, commit, etc. However, the bridge gets blown up when
files get (re)moved in the subversion repository.

> Is there a better version control system than
> SVN for handling the problem of person A changing
> file X out from under person B's uncommitted changes?
> I can't imagine how it could be handled other than
> side-channel communication (barring mind reading).

Git hashes all the files. So, if you

mv foo bar

and commit, bar has the same hash as foo and so git knows that edits
to bar stem from the history of foo. Hashing is critical for something
like the Linux kernel that has so many people who could potentially
move a file out from under someone else. As far as svn is concerned,
bar appears via immaculate conception.

I'm not strongly advocating switching to git, although I do think it
would have been a better choice to start with and maybe it is
something to think about after stan 1.0 is released. For now, I think
we could get by if disruptive changes were pre-announced with at least
24 hours notice.

Ben

messages.subject: Organization of Stan examples
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

We are running the BUGS examples we have every morning through our
continuous build server. See http://d1m1s1b1.stat.columbia.edu:8080/
for results.

In order for this to work properly, I have been relying on an
organization of the model file and data. If you are building Stan
models, could you follow these rules?

1) Only working Stan models should be named *.stan.
 - If you have a non-working model, it is ok to be in the directory.
Just call it something other than .stan
2) Data for the Stan model should be named the same with name with the
extension .Rdata.
  - Example: the rats example is in
src/models/bugs_examples/vol1/rats/rats.stan. Within the same folder
there is a rats.Rdata file.
  - If there are two different models within the same directory and
they require the same data, the data should be copied. If we had a
rats2.stan, we should have a rats2.Rdata.

To run the rats example, from the command line you can type:
> make models/bugs_examples/vol1/rats/rats.stan
and it will compile demo/gm, pipe the stan model through the
generator, compile the generated C++ code, and run the model.

In some of them we have additional files such as R scripts and
makefiles. They don't do any harm by being in the folder. If the
makefile is doing the steps above and nothing else, I would prefer to
remove them.

Daniel

> more simply, what ISN'T a disruptive change?  Is it
> just something that'll disrupt a local merge?  So it'd
> include swapping order of functions in a file, renaming

Yeah, I'd say "likely to disrupt the merge" is disruptive, albeit
subjective. There are big parts of Stan that only Bob works on, so for
example, there is not much chance of his changes to the parser
disrupting someone else. Conversely, moving all the files in prob to
somewhere in univariate vs. multivariate and discrete vs. continuous
subfolders could have bitten anyone (and did bite me).

> How about what Daniel just did, which was a wholesale
> replacement of "unsigned int" with either "size_t"
> or "vector<T>::size_type" as appropriate?

That seems non-disruptive because it is unlikely anyone else would be
changing unsigned int to int, although it could happen. I would say
that changing files is usually non-disruptive and changing the file
structure is usually disruptive (unless you are just adding purely new
files).

There is no perfect solution, and even under git / hg / bzr etc. you
get merge conflicts where 2 people change the same part of the same
file in different ways. But the post-subversion VCS have mechanisms to
minimize and resolve merge conflicts.

Ben

messages.subject: parallel RNG & gradient testing
messages.body_plain:
The gradient testing now happens after user
or random inits.  And it also now prints out
the param values as well as the gradients.

I decided it'd be easier to just go ahead and
implement the parallel RNG stuff so I could
stop worrying about it.  It'll also look better
in the paper.s

I just committed a version that uses parallel
random number generation a la L'Ecuyer.  The
--help option on a compiled model gives you
the options, but the relevant ones here are:

   --seed=<int>
   --chain_id=<int>

So if you're running 4 parallel chains, give them
each different ids, starting from 1.

The period for L'Ecuyer is around 2**61.  I back-of-the-enveloped
a skip-ahead (aka discard) of 2**50 (1 trillion) samples per chain,
allowing us 2**11 (2 thousand) distinct parallel chains.
So if they give us chain ID of 27, we skip ahead 27 * 2**50 samples
from the start of the chain with the given seed to start.

L'Ecuyer's method as implemented in Boost is about 8%
of the speed of the Mersenne Twister according to their
benchmarking, but it'd be easy enough to switch back or
even allow user specification of the random number generator.

Here's the original code for the Mersenne Twister:

   // FASTER, but no parallel guarantees
   // typedef boost::mt19937 rng_t;
   // rng_t base_rng(static_cast<unsigned int>(random_seed
   //                                          + chain_id - 1));

   typedef boost::ecuyer1988 rng_t;
   rng_t base_rng(chain_random_seed);
   // (2**50 = 1T samples, 1000 chains)
   static boost::uintmax_t DISCARD_STRIDE = 1 << 50;
   base_rng.discard(DISCARD_STRIDE * (chain_id - 1));

   ...

   stan::mcmc::nuts<rng_t> sampler(model, delta, -1, base_rng);

There's no RNG base class with virtual methods, which is
why the code looks how it does with typedefs.  This design's
faster because of no virtual functions, but a bit more of a pain
to plug and play -- if we want to allow the user to specify
which one they use, I'll need to template out a subroutine
based on the type of the RNG.  It would have been convenient
had they gone with the curiously recurring template pattern
like Eigen does for matrices.

- Bob

messages.subject: need help with Wishart
messages.body_plain:
I'm totally baffled by our Wishart and after two days
am finally out of ideas on how to approach debugging
it.  I'll need help from someone who's better at matrices
than me to figure this out.

We only tested the round-trip behavior of the transform,
not its derivatives.  So Ben's hypothesis that it might
be a problem with the Jacobian in the transform is still
a possibility.

A big problem for me is that I have no clue what the bits of
Ben's transform code mean.

We've checked the definitions of the Wishart a gazillion
times and  they pass all our unit tests checking against
MCMCpack.

I could just add 2 to the DOF and everything works the
way it should, which is really really puzzling.

I'm beginning to wonder if everyone copied the
wrong form of the density from each other.  It's
a long shot, but here's my reasoning.

There's a term in the log probability

    lp += multiply_log(0.5 * (nu - k - 1.0), determinant(W));

where

    multiply_log(x,y) == x * log(y);

BDA, Bishop's machine learning book, and the Wikipedia
all agree on the sign of 1 in this term.
And the results using this definition agree with MCMCpack, which
is how we generated unit tests.

Furthermore, everyone agrees the expectation is the dof
times the scale matrix.  But our posterior mean is
(dof - 2) * scale matrix.

There's a serious right skew to the posterior, but
I can't believe it's just a failure to sample outliers
as the results so consistently match what we should get
with two fewer degrees of freedom.

So what if instead of (nu - k - 1), the term were
(nu - (k - 1))?

It gives us right answer from sampling.  It effectively
adds 2 to the degrees of freedom, and previously it
was behaving as if the dof were 2 less than specified,
so getting the right posterior mean with this hack
in itself isn't surprising.

The suggested term (nu - (k - 1)) has the property that

1.  It will be great when we can run from R.  Then the data files will look much cleaner.

(b) Suppose we're fitting many different models from the same data.  Then it would be convenient to have a single data declaration and parameters block, and to swap in different models. messages.subject: proposal for inv_logit bounding
messages.body_plain:
In order to not send the Bernoulli 0 or 1
probabilities, I can redefine inv_logit so that
it behaves as follows:

   inv_logit(double x_b) {
     if (x_b < MIN) return 0.0001;
     if (x_b > MAX) return 0.9999;
     return 1/(1 + exp(-x_b));
   }

With this definition, the derivative will never
be zero or 1 either:

   d/dx inv_logit(x)
   = inv_logit(x) * (1 - inv_logit(x))

Instead, it'll be .0001 * .9999.

If we did this naively, as in using this in Stan
directly

   theta <- fmax(0.0001,fmin(0.9999,inv_logit(x_b)));

then we'd detach x_b from theta in the derivatie
calc when x_b was too large or small.

And if we did this, we'd get zeros:

   theta <- 0.0001 + 0.9999 * inv_logit(x_b);

I checked and neither really helps.

I'm heading out now, but I'll give it a whirl tomorrow.

I did manage to fit the data using Stan as is, but
it's painful.  It produces three coefficients near
0, one near -1 and one near 2.   Partly that may be
because the input data's not scaled -- the percentages
are between 0 and 100 (they really ARE percentages).

- Bob

I agree that having multiple names for the same thing is not good. My
fav help page in all of R is help(double) .

Also, if stan is 100% templated, why not support at least as many
precisions as Eigen does? Not that anyone should want single
precision, but someone might want *more* precision. In other words,
one way out of the problem we are facing with this logit model might
be to do

model {
  long double mu;
  for (i in 1:I) {
    mu = b_0 + b_1 * x_1[i] + b_2 * x_2[i] ... ;
    y[i] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(mu));
  }
}

That is not a very good solution because long double is highly
compiler dependent; see

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_double

And if I change inv_logit() to use expl() instead of exp(), it doesn't
help noticeably under g++. But it was a plausible idea.

Ben

messages.subject: Makefile updated
messages.body_plain:
I spent the last 2 days really working through the makefile. I think
it's in a better state now. At the very least, I understand make much
better.

The changes should not really affect how you currently build.

The biggest changes are:
- separate variable declarations for the 3 operating systems
- dependencies are autogenerated

If you want OS specific flags, there are 3 files (mac, win, linux)
under src/makefile that set specific flags based on the OS. The OS is
automatically detected, but to force it from the command line, set the
variable OS to either mac, win, or linux.

The result of the dependencies being autogenerated should help us with
compile time for unit tests. We shouldn't need to clean before running
the unit tests again. Any changes to source files will trickle down
and force recompilation of any test that requires it. Also, the target
is now "test-unit". I have left "test-all" in there as the same
target, but my intention is to have "test-all" run a more
comprehensive test in the future.

The test-bugs target runs all the bugs examples. This is what Jenkins
runs in the mornings. It is not currently able to finish all bugs
models. I am working through them slowly so we can detect when changes
to the code base stop our models from running.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: basic logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
Adding precision to a Stan model is an interesting
idea.  It would be easier to support at the whole
model level than variable by variable (a problem
with the latter being Eigen's not wanting to do
things like multiply double matrices by float
or long double matrices).  I haven't templated out
the double type, but it'd be relatively straightforward.

I like the idea of calling it "real" rather than
"double" in the code.

The problem is exp(x), which for doubles, only allows a
domain of x in roughly (-750,750).  Values of x that
are too small result in underflow to 0 and
too big result in overflow to +infinity.
This means that

    inv_logit(x) = 1/(1+exp(-x))

inherits the same domain for x, but where under-
and over-flow result in 0 or 1 values.

For logistic regression, the problem is that we
don't get that much additional range going from
64 to 128 bits.  It only increases the exponent
from 11 bits to 15 bits, which gives us log(2**4)
or about triple the range, or around (-2000,2000).
We do get a whole lot more precision in the base
number, though :-)

- Bob

On 2/11/12 10:10 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Feb 11, 9:16 pm, Bob Carpenter<c...@alias-i.com>  wrote:
>> On 2/11/12 9:10 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>>> 4.  For naive users such as myself, would it be useful to have "real" alias for "double"?  I'm assuming all our reals are actually double-precision, i.e. there's no "single" category, so it could be convenient to have "real" with the manual noting that it's an alias for "double".  Or am I missing something there?
>>
>> I'd rather just call it one thing rather than have
>> two aliases.  I'm happy to go with real.  There isn't
>> going to be single-precision or quadruple-precision options.
>
> I agree that having multiple names for the same thing is not good. My
> fav help page in all of R is help(double) .
>
> Also, if stan is 100% templated, why not support at least as many
> precisions as Eigen does? Not that anyone should want single
> precision, but someone might want *more* precision. In other words,
> one way out of the problem we are facing with this logit model might
> be to do
>
> model {
>    long double mu;
>    for (i in 1:I) {
>      mu = b_0 + b_1 * x_1[i] + b_2 * x_2[i] ... ;
>      y[i] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(mu));
>    }
> }
>
> That is not a very good solution because long double is highly
> compiler dependent; see
>
> http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_double
>
> And if I change inv_logit() to use expl() instead of exp(), it doesn't
> help noticeably under g++. But it was a plausible idea.
>
> Ben
>
>

messages.subject: "real" it is
messages.body_plain:
"double" isn't any more jargony than "real".
Both have specific meanings and "double" is
more accurate in this case.  Real
numbers are a mathematical concept whereas
double-precision floating point is an approximate
implementation.  The Stan variables declared
as doubles are implemented as doubles.

Having said that, I like the idea of expressing
the models mathematically and letting the Stan
compiler sort out the implementation details.
As Ben pointed out, we could always change the
nature of our real-number approximation without
changing the Stan code.

So, "real" it is.

- Bob

held anything other than real numbers in them.

 > boost::math::policies::policy

 > ...

There are at least three instances of default_policy
in play:

A.  The un-namespaced typedef of default_policy inside of

   agrad/error_handling_test.cpp

B.  Boost's default_policy struct defined in

   http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_48_0/boost/math/policies/policy.hpp

C. Stan's default_policy defined in stan/maths/error_handling.hpp.

The test file then has a "using namespace stan::maths" which brings
in (C) on top of (A).

Some fixes that should take care of the problem:

1.  Remove "using namespace stan::maths" from the test file.
Don't ever use a namespace -- just bring in functions.

2.  Rename the typedef in the stan::maths namespace
in stan/maths/error_handling.hpp to something
other than "default_policy".

3.  Rename the typedef in agrad/error_handling_test.cpp to something
other than "default_policy" (or remove it and just
use the one from the stan::maths namespace).

- Bob

messages.subject: Stan Beta release
messages.body_plain:
I'm thinking we should start with an official
beta release at the end of February.  That's to let
people know things may be a bit rough for the
first few users until we see how things go.

Other than doc (which is what I'm focusing on
now), the only remaining necessary code to-do
items are:

   -- discrete slice sampler for unbounded
      integer parameters

   -- diagonal mass matrix estimation

I'm more concerned about the latter than the
former given our trouble with scaling in Ben's
logistic regression example.

There are also a whole bunch of nice-to-have
items relating to efficiency and a few related
to easier debugging.

Also, should I be recording the total log
probability function value in each saved iteration
along with the samples?  It's not a parameter and
we don't really want to test its convergence,
but it might be nice to include.

And of course, there's an actual R interface
instead of the file-based round-trips we have now.

- Bob

messages.subject: HMC/NUTS sampler config for Stan
messages.body_plain:
I'd like to be able to configure our (auto-tuned) HMC/NUTS
by choosing one item from each of the following lists:

   1.  a. specify fixed step size
       b. specify interval of step sizes
       c. adapt fixed step size
       d. adapt interval of step sizes

   2.  a. specify fixed number of steps
       b. NUTS adaptation for number of steps

I think it'll be easiest to configure this with command-line
options of:

   --step-size
   -----------------
   Set to fixed step size (turn off step size auto tuning)

   --step-interval
   --------------------
   Sample in interval from (1-val)*size to (1+val)*size.

   --steps
   -------
   Set fixed number of steps (turn off NUTS number of steps adaptation)

This leads to the following params for the above
cases:

   1.a.  { --step-size }
   1.b.  { --step-size, --step-interval }
   1.c.  { }
   1.d.  { --step-interval }

   2.a   { --steps }
   2.b.  { }

This would lead to the two extreme configs:

   Basic NUTS as in the paper/talk:  { }

   Basic HMC:  { --step-size, --steps }

and the one Radford likes:

   Basic HMC w. interval:  { --step-size, --step-interval, --steps }

If no one objects, I'll see if I can push this through
the code.  I don't think there'll be an easy way to avoid
a big "if" on the NUTS vs. no-NUTS.

- Bob

>      c. adapt fixed step size
>      d. adapt interval of step sizes
>
>  2.  a. specify fixed number of steps
>      b. NUTS adaptation for number of steps
>
> I think it'll be easiest to configure this with command-line
> options of:
>
>  --step-size
>  -----------------
>  Set to fixed step size (turn off step size auto tuning)
>
>  --step-interval
>  --------------------
>  Sample in interval from (1-val)*size to (1+val)*size.
>
>  --steps
>  -------
>  Set fixed number of steps (turn off NUTS number of steps adaptation)
>
> This leads to the following params for the above
> cases:
>
>  1.a.  { --step-size }
>  1.b.  { --step-size, --step-interval }
>  1.c.  { }
>  1.d.  { --step-interval }
>
>  2.a   { --steps }
>  2.b.  { }
>
> This would lead to the two extreme configs:
>
>  Basic NUTS as in the paper/talk:  { }
>
>  Basic HMC:  { --step-size, --steps }
>
> and the one Radford likes:
>
>  Basic HMC w. interval:  { --step-size, --step-interval, --steps }
>
> If no one objects, I'll see if I can push this through
> the code.  I don't think there'll be an easy way to avoid
> a big "if" on the NUTS vs. no-NUTS.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: Re: SVN to Git
messages.body_plain:
The git documentation at

http://git-scm.com/documentation

is pretty good, whatever your taste in documentation may be.
Basically, for everything worthwhile in svn, there is a corresponding
git command. However, there are worthwhile features of git that are
not in svn, so you have to remind yourself to make use of them. You
can see most of the commands by doing

master!stan-git> git --help
usage: git [--version] [--exec-path[=<path>]] [--html-path] [--man-
path] [--info-path]
           [-p|--paginate|--no-pager] [--no-replace-objects] [--bare]
           [--git-dir=<path>] [--work-tree=<path>] [--
namespace=<name>]
           [-c name=value] [--help]
           <command> [<args>]

The most commonly used git commands are:
   add        Add file contents to the index
   bisect     Find by binary search the change that introduced a bug
   branch     List, create, or delete branches
   checkout   Checkout a branch or paths to the working tree
   clone      Clone a repository into a new directory
   commit     Record changes to the repository
   diff       Show changes between commits, commit and working tree,
etc
   fetch      Download objects and refs from another repository
   grep       Print lines matching a pattern
   init       Create an empty git repository or reinitialize an
existing one
   log        Show commit logs
   merge      Join two or more development histories together
   mv         Move or rename a file, a directory, or a symlink
   pull       Fetch from and merge with another repository or a local
branch
   push       Update remote refs along with associated objects
   rebase     Forward-port local commits to the updated upstream head
   reset      Reset current HEAD to the specified state
   rm         Remove files from the working tree and from the index
   show       Show various types of objects
   status     Show the working tree status
   tag        Create, list, delete or verify a tag object signed with
GPG

See 'git help <command>' for more information on a specific command.

Many of these subcommands have a --dry-run that you can use if you are
unsure of what will happen. It is almost always possible to roll
mistakes back but that requires careful understanding of the relevant
documentation.

If you use Emacs, there is also some helpful Emacs modes and stuff at

http://www.emacswiki.org/emacs/Git

The main difference is that whereas development under svn primarily
takes place in "the" trunk, development under git takes place
primarily in local branches (plural). When the conversion goes down
Friday, there will at first be just a "master" branch. But I would
strongly favor a rule that no one should edit source code directly in
the master branch. Maybe we can update TODO, add code comments, etc.
directly in the master branch, but the main thing is that the master
branch should never, ever be broken because everyone (possibly
including random people on the internet that we don't even know about)
will be branching off our master branch.

To create a local branch from master and switch to it, do

git checkout master
git branch foo
git checkout foo

At this moment in time, foo is identical to master. Once you start
making changes to foo, then it diverges from master but can be merged
back into master (possibly much) later on. Pretend you have made some
changes to the files in stan and saved them to the hard disk. Git
actually doesn't care at this point. If you do

git status

it will tell you those files have been modified and if you do

git diff

you can see the diff relative to the last *committed* change. To be
relevant, you have to "add" the modified files to the staging area so
that they can subsequently be committed locally. The use of the word
"add" is a bit confusing because it is the same word regardless of
whether you are adding a brand new file from scratch or adding a
modified file that already exists in the tree to the staging area. In
other words, you are "adding a file to the staging area", not
necessarily "adding a file to the tree". If you just do

git add .

(note there is a "dot" in the last line) it will add all modified
files to the staging area. This is often not what you want either
because you only want to add a particular modified file to the staging
area or because make test-all has created a lot of temporary binary
junk that does not (and should not) be tracked by git. So you can
instead do

git add path/to/modified/file.hpp

or

git add path/to/directory/where/modified/files/are

to do a more tailored adding of files to the staging area.

At that point, you can do

git commit -m "commit message" -m "optional longer commit explanation"

or if you omit the last half, git will open $EDITOR so that you can
write a commit message. Tradition dictates that there should be one
line explaining the commit, optionally followed by two line breaks and
one or more paragraphs explaining the commit in more detail. At this
point, the modifications are committed to the local branch but your
local branch is not (yet) relevant to anyone else. You can iterate the
process of adding to the staging area and locally committing in order
to make smaller and more self-contained steps. But if you know that
you have just made a few changes that you want to all be staged in a
single commit, you could instead streamline the above by doing

git commit -a -m "commit message" -m "optional longer commit
explanation"

which would add with the -a flag ALL modified files to the staging
area and commit them as a group to the local branch.

You can and should have multiple local branches. For example, I have
the following branches now

master!stan-git> git branch -a
  BB
  ice
  lkj
  logit
* master
  multinormal
  policy
  remotes/git-svn

So, I have a branch where I was working on the BetaBinomial several
weeks ago, a branch where I was trying to figure out WTF was up with
the ice example in BUGS. A branch with ongoing work on the LKJ
transformation / distribution. The master branch which currently
tracks to the svn trunk. A branch with stuff on multivariate normal. A
branch with my hapless attempt to figure out that bug with policy
under g++-4.4. Since Bob / Daniel fixed that bug, now would be a good
time to delete that branch with

master!stan-git> git branch -d policy
Deleted branch policy (was 3f2631e).

So, basically my hacking around with that policy thing never happened
as far as you all are concerned. There is also the non-local branch
remotes/git-svn which tracks the svn trunk. This will be called
remotes/master when the conversion goes down; i.e. there is a master
branch in a certain state on the Google Code server and the "same"
master branch --- possibly in a different state very temporarily ---
on each of our machines.

Basically, the moral of the story is that you should create a local
branch every time you want to accomplish some halfway well-defined
goal with the code. So, if we were using git yesterday, Bob would
likely have made a better_debugging local branch, an inv_logit local
branch, a more_nuts_options local branch, and possibly some other
branches that the rest of us don't even need to know about. Another
good principle is not to let a branch drift from its original purpose.
Say Bob is implementing the features in the more_nuts_options branch
and discovers some unrelated bug. It would be better to

git checkout master
git branch unrelated_bug
git checkout unrelated_bug

and fix, test, etc. the unrelated bug in its branch, rather than
lumping it in with the rest of the stuff in the more_nuts_options
branch. One reason for this is that it is clearer, but the main reason
is that it may take a LONG time before Bob is happy enough with the
(more invasive) more_nuts_options branch to merge it back into the
master branch, whereas the fix to the unrelated bug should get pushed
to the master branch as soon as it is thoroughly fixed. There is an
option called "cherry picking" where Bob could extract and push just
the commits that fix the unrelated bug, but that is a bit messy.

I would say that the leading cause of problems with git is forgetting
which branch you are currently working on and / or remembering that
you have made some changes to the code but forgetting that those
changes were actually made to a different branch than the one you are
currently working on. You can configure your shell prompt to remind
you the branch name, but it is still easy to overlook. One place where
this manifests itself is accidentally branching from another local
branch instead of from the (local) master branch. Say Bob is working
on the more_nuts_options branch when he discovers the unrelated bug.
If he just does

git branch unrelated_bug
git checkout unrelated_bug

then the unrelated_bug branch will branch off of more_nuts_options
instead of master. Occasionally, you want to branch from a local
branch (... from a local branch)^n but most of the time, inclusive of
this case, you want to branch from the (local) master branch. If
unrelated_bug branches from more_nuts_options, then the commits that
Bob makes to fix the unrelated bug will be on top of Bob's half-baked
commits that implement more NUTS options. In that case, merging the
fix to the unrelated bug to master would also merge in the half-baked
commits implementing more NUTS options and thus the master branch
would be in a less-than-perfect state.

I've mentioned "merging" a few times already, which can get a bit
frustrating. When a branch is "done", meaning at a minimum you are
happy with it, all the tests pass, the stuff is documented if
necessary, etc. then you have to merge it back so that the rest of the
world can use it. There may be better ways but these are the steps I
do with the mi package.

# STEP 1: Sync your local master branch to the state of the master
branch on Google Code (origin)

git checkout master
git pull origin master

This is because during the time that Bob was working on
more_nuts_options, Matt may have fully implemented nutsN and pushed it
to Google Code, so Bob needs to catch up with that. Actually, people
should execute those two lines often, just to see what other people
have done, which is easy with some of the graphical tools or

git log

# STEP 2: Merge the local master branch into the local feature branch

git checkout more_nuts_options
git merge . master

(note that there is a "dot" in the last line). This ostensibly lays
Matt's work on top of Bob's work. In practice, there often is a "merge
conflict", which is annoying but usually is easily fixed. A merge
conflict happens when Matt and Bob change the same line(s) of code in
different ways. In this case, git will say something like "there is a
merge conflict in file.hpp, commit a fix and do git merge --continue
or you can do git merge --abort". At that point, if you do

git diff path/to/conflicted/file.hpp

you will see that git has inserted some markers indicating where the
conflict is and stacked the two sets of changes on top of each other.
The diff will look something like

>>>>>BOB>>>>>
- x = 1;
+ x = 2;
>>>>>MATT>>>>
- x = 1;
+ x = 3;
>>>>>>>>>>>>>

except it doesn't actually say BOB and MATT but rather HEAD (this
refers to the state of Bob's more_nuts_options branch) and a SHA
string (this refers to the SHA of the last commit that Matt pushed to
the master branch on Google Code). The >>> business actually is there
and facilitates finding the conflicts in large files. At this point,
Bob has to decide whether x should be 2 or 3 (or anything else), erase
all the lines that git inserted, commit to the more_nuts_options
branch and do

git merge --continue

to continue the mergification of other files that may have diverged.

Sometimes, there will be a huge merge conflict where multiple people
do fundamentally different things to the same code. In this situation,
it may be best to

git merge --abort

which will leave more_nuts_options in the state it was before the
aborted merge. Then, Bob and Matt can talk / email about which
direction to go. So, merge conflicts inevitably happen with multiple
developers, branches, etc. going on but because they are anticipated,
it is usually not too hard to resolve them.

Assuming the resolution of all merge conflicts, Bob can go onto

# STEP 3: Make an "empty" commit explaining what the more_nuts_options
branch accomplished

git commit --allow-empty

this will launch $EDITOR to allow Bob to write a longer commit message
even though no code has changed since the commit(s) that merged master
into more_nuts_options. So Bob could write something like:

"The more_nuts_options branch implements more NUTS options as follows

--foo does foo
--bar does bar
--baz does baz

The reason for these changes is because it is a good idea in one or
more of the following situations ..."

Not everybody does step 3 but I think it is a good practice because
when somebody is scrolling through the log it will give them a place
to get an overview of the branch, as opposed to wading through the
tens or hundreds of small commits in the more_nuts_options branch that
actually implement more NUTS options. Probably it wouldn't be
necessary if the purpose of the branch was just to fix some bug.

# STEP 4: Merge the more_nuts_options branch into the local master
branch

git checkout master
git merge . more_nuts_options

(note there is a "dot" in the last line). This step should never
generate a merge conflict because more_nuts_options already has
everything from master (with any merge conflicts resolved at this
point) and more_nuts_options just has the extra "empty" commit giving
an overview of more_nuts_options.

# STEP 5: Sync the master branch on Google Code with your local master
branch

git push origin master

Make double, super, extra sure that you are in your local master
branch before pushing to the master branch on Google Code. In other
words, you really don't want to accidentally be in some half-baked
branch and push that to the master branch on Google Code because then
everyone else would be branching from a polluted master branch.

# STEP 6: Optionally delete the local feature branch

git branch -d more_nuts_options

Since everything from the more_nuts_options branch is now not only in
the local master branch but also the master branch on Google Code, the
more_nuts_options branch isn't needed, although it doesn't hurt
anything to keep it around for a little while longer in case a problem
is discovered.

Some people have different ideas about the best workflow and
procedures. One possible rule is that "Only Bob gets to merge into the
master branch"; this is basically the rule they use for the Linux
kernel where Bob = Linus. Under that rule, everybody else would push
their local branches to Google Code when they are ostensibly ready.
For example, Matt would do steps 1, 2, and 3 and then

git push origin nutsN

at which point the Google Code server would (or at least should, I
have never actually done this with Google Code) have both "our" master
branch and Matt's nutsN branch. At which point, Matt would communicate
to Bob that he should look at and merge the nutsN branch to the master
branch, which Bob would do with

git pull origin nutsN
git checkout nutsN

After Bob verifies that nutsN is in good shape (and / or possibly
makes some more commits to it), Bob could merge the nutsN branch into
the master branch by following steps 4 and 5 above.

I don't know if we need to have a rule that says "Only Bob gets to
merge into the master branch". It would help Bob keep up to speed with
what other people are doing, but it also makes more work for him. If
the test suite is good and people are very careful to not break the
master branch, then we could do without it.

In either case, pushing a local branch to Google Code and sending an
email to the list saying "Can someone pull, help with, test my
potentially invasive changes" can be useful, in which case the second
person could edit / stage / commit to the local copy of that branch
and push to the first person's remote branch on Google Code (instead
of master) whereupon the first person can merge that remote branch
back into his local branch. Taking this to its logical extreme, some
projects do "peer review" where the first person announces that a
branch is available for review, a second person (not necessarily Bob)
approves of it or not, and if so, either the first or second person
merges into the master branch. This can work well if there are
multiple people who understand the same parts of the code and thus can
do good reviewing. I don't know if we could pull that off.

Winding down, one very useful command is

git grep REGEX DIR

which quickly finds all occurrences of the regular expression in or
under DIR. Often DIR would be src/ because you usually don't want
matches from Boost or Eigen in lib/ .

Also, if you do need to (re)move a file, make sure to use one of

git rm path/to/first_file.hpp
git mv path/to/second_file.hpp
git commit -a -m "(re)moving some files"

so that git can reconcile everything when those commits get pushed
into the master branch and subsequently pulled by other people with
potentially conflicting branches, etc.

Finally, because development under git is not chronological, it is not
possible to refer to "revision 793" because there is no such thing as
of Friday. But many of the commands have the option of operating on
specific commits. So git hashes every single commit, and you can refer
to it by the SHA. For example, in my git log, I see that r793 is
officially known as dee...

commit dee7347823ab7ae9a9e90a36991796fcafb5c68f
Author: bea...@alum.mit.edu <bea...@alum.mit.edu@9a304bd9-dce1-
f7c0-8d5c-bb1642157d4e>
Date:   Thu Feb 16 23:30:01 2012 +0000

    removed warning in printf.

THE END

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Git hooks
messages.body_plain:
At a variety of places, git can call a script before taking action.
One such hook is called "pre-commit". I have done

cp .git/hooks/pre-commit.sample .git/hooks/pre-commit

then I commented out the last line (which prohibits trailing
whitespace) and added this line

exec make CC=clang++ 0=3 -j8 test-all > /dev/null

This way, if one of the tests fails, I can't commit my saved changes
to my local repository.

Under a more Subversion-based paradigm, it would seem better for the
central server to reject commits that cause tests to fail, but as far
as I know, Google Code does not allow projects to run unit tests on
Google's servers. So, it might seem better to have a pre-push hook on
the client side, but the Git developers have never agreed on whether
pre-push hooks are appropriate given the alternatives.

Thus, even though rejecting a commit because it fails a test seems a
bit extreme, that seems like the best we can do for now. Also, you can
skip the pre-commit hook by passing -n to git commit, so you can thus
commit broken stuff if you really want to. Are there other things that
we should do in the pre-commit hook or other hooks?

Ben

messages.subject: R interface via Rcpp
messages.body_plain:
I finally understand how we can use "Rcpp package" to
build an R interface for Stan.  Rcpp's much more
powerful than I first thought, though the documentation
is spread over several fragmentary pdfs.

Package: Stan
----

This is going to involve one basic function, stan(),
playing the role of bugs() in R2WinBUGS.  The
signature is going to be something like:

   StanSamples

   stan(model,data,inits,
        iter,warmup,thin,
        ... NUTS or HMC params ...,
        ... misc. params ...)

This will have to do a number of things which can be broken
out as sub-functions:

a.  If the model hasn't been compiled, compile it using
     the stanc compiler (what's now in demo/gm).  We can
     call the compiler from R using Rcpp.

b.  If not already done, generate boilerplate around
     the generated C++ model code to link it up with
     Stan C++ to create a model-specific  Rcpp package on the
     fly.

c.  Dynamically (re)link the newly created package, which
     corresponds to the model.

d.  Run the sampler (perhaps in multiple threads), and
     save the results to a Coda-like C++ object which we make available
     to R through Rcpp.

What's neat is that the implementation of (d) in C++
rather than in R means we can make Stan scalable beyond
what we could do if we had a Coda-like object in R.
Only the data that's being used need be brought into an R
representation.  Of course, if you wind up bringing it all
in at once, that'll be less efficient, because now we have
all the R baggage and the C++ object.

It'll also mean no huge lag after sampling's done while all the
data gets marshaled in R.

This does mean we'd write things like ESS and WAIC
and split-R-hat in C++.  This should make them faster.
And more portable (looks like the Rcpp package functionality
was based on Boost.Python, so maybe Python will be easy to
knock off next if all the heavy lifting (other than plotting)
is on the C++ side).

What I'd like to get some help with (Ben?  Jiqiang?  Malecki?)
is

1.  setting up the R package boilerplate and figuring out where
everything needs to go like C++ compiler options and linked
libraries for Rcpp, and

2.  writing the plotting commands in R and working with Andrew
to make them acceptable.  There are three pieces to this, I think.
The basic plot() to summarize all the resulting posterior intervals
(edited to fit on one plot) and R-hat/ESS values, posterior plots
for individual or paired variables, and traceplots per variable (or
for pairs?).

- Bob

The stanc compiler is a C++ program that converts
the text file Stan model to another text file containing
C++.  No C++ compilation or linking required here.

When we need to compile/link the generated C++ code,
the Rcpp package approach seems neat.  The trick is
going to be using something that can dynamically link
and later re-link when the user changes the model.

> x86-64 that are used for C++ compiler options as documented at
>
> http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html#Using-Makevars

Malecki did that (I did watch!).  But I don't understand
what all of this stuff needs to be.

have some more concrete questions.

messages.subject: Rstan: naming, system, etc.
messages.body_plain:
1.  Naming

I'm with Andrew that we should call the package:

    Stan

Though I like caps.

That confuses the code organization a bit now, as
we have a directory:

    stan/rstan/rstan

with all of the R stuff in it.  How about changing
the name of that to:

    stan/R/stan

?

2.  I'm looking at the stan.R code that Ben inserted.
It uses a system() call.  Is this going to work cross
platform?  That's where I was imagining we'd have a
compile command implemented through Rcpp so that the
compiler ran in the same process as R itself.

If we do a system call, we need to worry about supplying
an executable or having users compile the code.

Given our problems with Windows compilers, this may turn
out to be easier than compiling through R(cpp).

I don't understand the design decisions well enough here.

3.  Is inline related to Rcpp in any way other than having
the same author?  I did find this blog of John Cook's:

http://www.johndcook.com/blog/2011/06/30/calling-cpp-from-r/

- Bob

That is okay, although has the confusion that a directory will be stan/
R/stan/R/ .

But I am not sure we should change the name of the R package to stan.
The dominant naming convention for R packages that interface with
external software is to have R or R2 or something in the name
(R2WinBUGS, RcppEigen, etc.). If you ever intend to have them packaged
for Linux distributions, having two source packages with the same name
will cause some headaches. Finally, since stan the library is BSD and
stan the R package is GPL, I'd say that having distinct names would be
less legally confusing.

> 2.  I'm looking at the stan.R code that Ben inserted.
> It uses a system() call.  Is this going to work cross
> platform?  That's where I was imagining we'd have a
> compile command implemented through Rcpp so that the
> compiler ran in the same process as R itself.

Yes. Nowdays there is system2() which is more portable in a sense but
was only introduced into R a couple of years ago.

> If we do a system call, we need to worry about supplying
> an executable or having users compile the code.

Executable what exactly? Executables like demo/gm should exist once
the user installs the R package (whether they build it from source or
install the binary R package). For executables like particular models,
then the user would have to compile them, in which case on Windows
they need the Rtools toolchain (not VisualStudio).

> 3.  Is inline related to Rcpp in any way other than having
> the same author?  I did find this blog of John Cook's:

Most of the code in the inline package was originally written by Oleg
Sklyar. The inline package is a suggestency of the Rcpp package
because some R functions in Rcpp utilize inline.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Rstan: naming, system, etc.
messages.body_plain:
OK, this would probably be easier if I just came to the stan meeting. When is that?

What I had in my head was that the R package would have an inst/include/ directory that basically contained stan/src/. When the R package gets installed (from source), the installation would essentially involve a "make demo/gm". That is essentially what the RcppEigen package does. The binary version of the R package (built from source by / on CRAN's servers) would thus have the demo/gm executable.

Once the R package is installed and loaded, the main stan() function would use the system() or system2() function to pass a .stan text file to demo/gm to yield the C++ file, which would then get processed by Rcpp's magic. Then, the main stan() function would use the .Call() function in R to pass the data to the just-compiled model and execute.

But there are probably other ways to do it as well.

Ben
